column2: A 1930s rubber-hose cartoon, the black-and-white era of Fleischer and early Disney shorts (all characters your own invention: no Mickey, Betty Boop, Felix or Cuphead). PAIR: ink black #141210 on film cream #efe6cf. The four numerals ARE the cast: each digit is a rubber-hose character whose body is the numeral's own shape (the bowl of a 6 is its belly, a 7 leans like a lanky fellow), with pie-cut eyes, white-glove hands and noodle arms and legs drawn as clean 2-3 px ink lines, big shoes; design all ten as characters that still read first as digits at --scale 4 (limbs thin and kept outside the counters, never closing a bowl or making 1 read 7). The whole picture lives on the cartoon's famous beat: everything (digits, the flowers, the clouds, a lamppost, the moon) bounces, squashes and stretches on a 2-frames-per-step jazz rhythm, about 2 beats a second, with a swing; between beats the digits dance (a heel-kick, a shimmy, a tip of the hat, two digits linking arms), every few seconds a bigger gag (one digit tap-dances a break, a cloud rains on one, the sun winks, a musical note flies out of a gramophone). Constant life in every frame, the digits included. Film texture is welcome as 1-bit: occasional vertical scratch, dust specks, a slight frame jitter of the background (never of the digits so much they misread), an iris ring at the edges. Minute turn, the centrepiece: the changing digit takes a bow and exits in classic style (a dash off-stage with speed lines and a dust puff, or a trapdoor drop), its slot gone before :00, and after :00 the new digit makes an entrance (pops out of a hat, swings in on a rope, drops in and squashes), landing on the beat. Hour: a bigger show: a full chorus line: all four digits kick in sync while the iris closes to a circle round them and opens again on a new set (day street, a farmyard, the moon at night), with a title card style hour in cartoon lettering, the time readable throughout.

Fire, the demoscene way: the classic 1-bit-friendly 'fire effect' (heat rising and cooling, flames licking upward) and a campfire's burning letters. PAIR: flame orange #ff7a1a ink on deep ember brown #1e0804 ground. The numerals are made of fire: each digit is a burning shape whose strokes are the hot core, the flames lick upward from every top edge and stroke in tongues that flicker every frame, sparks and embers rise and drift, and the stroke itself shimmers (a 1-bit dither of heat). Design all ten numerals as bold flame-carrying letterforms (like letters cut in a burning sign or written in a line of fuel) whose base shape stays crisp and readable at --scale 4 while their edges and tops are always alive; flames from one digit must never bridge into another or close a counter. Use a cheap closed-form flame field (scrolling integer noise with an upward advection and a cooling falloff, sampled on a coarse grid and dithered to 1 bit with an ordered pattern), not a simulation from boot. A heartbeat: once a second a gust makes every flame flare and lean, and every ~10 s a whoosh of sparks bursts out of one digit. The ground is not empty: rising heat shimmer, a few drifting embers, a dark silhouette of logs or a hearth grate at the bottom. Minute turn, the centrepiece: the old digit burns down: its flames climb higher and the stroke is eaten evenly along its whole length by charring (all of it thinning at once, never top to bottom, so it never reads as another digit), collapsing into glowing ash that blows away before :00; after :00 a spark runs along the new digit's whole path as a thin fuse, then it ignites and flares up to full fire. Hour: a bigger show: a flashover: fire sweeps across the whole strip as a wall of flame that leaves the new hour burning in its wake, or a firework of sparks spells and frames the hour, the time readable throughout. Night: the fire burns lower and redder in rhythm (backlight dims; the two colours stay).

Ferrofluid on a lab bench: black magnetic fluid that stands up into spikes (the Rosensweig instability) over hidden electromagnets. PAIR: ferrofluid black #0e1014 ink on pale lab-cyan light #c7e6ec ground (a lit glass dish). The numerals are pools of ferrofluid pulled into shape by magnets under the glass: each digit is a flat black silhouette whose edges and top are covered in sharp spikes that rise, sharpen and sink with the magnetic field, rippling along the strokes in waves (spikes are flat triangles in the 1-bit way, like the famous Kodama ferrofluid sculptures: no shading). Design all ten digits as bold pools with clean open counters, readable at --scale 4 whatever the spikes are doing (the spikes live on the outer edge and top only, never across a counter). Constant life in every frame: the field pulses to a beat (about once a second the spikes leap up together and relax), a slower wave travels along the strokes so the spikes rise in sequence like a crowd doing the wave, now and then a small droplet breaks off, crawls across the dish towards another magnet and merges again, and every ~10 s a bigger flourish (a spiral of spikes winds round one digit, or the whole fluid shivers). The ground stays calm: the dish rim, a few reflections as 1-bit lines, a faint grid of the magnet coils under the glass. Minute turn, the centrepiece: the changing digit's magnet switches off: its spikes collapse, the pool slumps and the fluid flows as a smooth blob along the dish (gone from its slot before :00, never passing through a shape that reads as another digit), then after :00 the new magnet switches on and the blob is pulled out into the new numeral, its outline first, then the spikes rising from it. Hour: a bigger show: the whole dish becomes a sculpture: all the fluid gathers in the centre into a rising, spinning spiked tower (a flat silhouette) that then spills outward and reforms all four digits of the new hour, the time readable throughout (keep blank under ~1 s).

An Amiga/Atari-ST demoscene 'cracktro' or intro screen, the most dynamic graphics of the 1980s: sine scrollers, bouncing logos, starfields, rasters, dithered plasma, all here in pure 1-bit. PAIR: hot magenta #ff2a9a ink on black #000000 ground. The time is the demo's big logo: four numerals in a bold chrome-free 1-bit display font of your own design (a demoscene logo face: thick, angular, with inline stripes or a checker fill, readable at --scale 4) that are always moving: they bob on a sine wave one after another, their inline stripes scroll through them, a raster bar of inverted lines slides down through them, they swing gently left and right like the classic bouncing logo (never so far they collide, never mirrored or narrowed, so they never misread). Around them the whole demo runs at full speed: a 1-bit starfield streaming past, a sine scroller across the bottom with a greeting text in your own 8x8 demo font (greetings to invented groups, no real names), a plasma or interference pattern in dither behind, a rotating flat checkerboard or tunnel of rings, a VU-meter equaliser bouncing to the imaginary chip tune's beat (about 2 beats a second, a kick that pulses everything). Never static, never subtle: but the time is the strongest read and the background is calmer than the logo (keep the pattern sparse behind the digits, or knock it out in a moat round them). Minute turn, the centrepiece: a demo effect swaps the digit: the old numeral explodes into pixels that fly out on sine paths (thinning evenly, gone before :00), and after :00 the new numeral zooms or is pixel-sorted in, or a vertical-blinds wipe reveals it. Hour: a bigger show: a full 'part change' as in a megademo: the screen flashes, the background effect switches (starfield to plasma to tunnel to vector balls in flat 1-bit dots), the hour digits come in with a big bounce, and the scroller announces the hour, the time readable throughout.
